title: Dalton Caldwell on how YC startup advice holds up in the age of AI
summary: Ex-YC partner Dalton Caldwell walks through classic YC advice (pick a non-obvious idea, build a simple MVP, talk to users, raise less, win by being unignorable) and how each updates with AI coding tools. Core theme: AI makes features and code cheap, so focus, direct user conversations and unconventional ideas matter more, not less.

principles.text: Obvious ideas on a new platform rarely become big outcomes; build something the new tech newly makes possible.
principles.quote: the really obvious App Store app ideas were kind of not good startups.

principles.text: Start from your unfair advantages and context, then apply them to the emerging technology.
principles.quote: you want to find the areas of context and advantages and then apply it to the emerging technology.

principles.text: With AI, code is easy for everyone; it must be paired with something inspired that delivers real user value.
principles.quote: anyone could write code some That is not enough. You have to combine that with something inspired, in my opinion, that delivers real value to users.

principles.text: Launch with one simple, explainable feature that solves a problem, then add rings around it. Cheap features don't change this.
principles.quote: do the hard thing first which is to make one feature that solves a problem for people and that they can explain back to you what the product is and why they want it

principles.text: Talk about what you're building publicly; most startups die from obscurity, not from being copied.
principles.quote: most startups die not because someone copied your idea, it's just because no one ever heard that you existed.

principles.text: Talk to users directly; 20-30 conversations beat thousands of ad-driven signups, and automating this loses nuance.
principles.quote: sitting down and talking to 20 or 30 people is going to give you more information about if you're on the right track or not than signing up 10,000 randos from Google Ads.
